forces: Boy soprano, string quartet, harp and organ
performers: Alain Fauqueur, boy soprano; J. J. Grunenwald, organ; members of the Orchestre des Concerts Lamoureux; Igor Markevitch, conductor
question: What changes when the unsettled organ writing gives way to the quiet major-key ending?
intro: A single high voice faces the organ’s restless harmony, with four strings and a harp rather than a full orchestra. Alain Fauqueur sings Boulanger’s last completed work; listen for how the small ensemble makes its final calm sound earned rather than automatic.

cues.title: A chamber prayer
cues.text: One singer, two violins, viola, cello, harp and organ make up this chamber score. There is no double-bass part and no chorus. Keep the organ’s moving harmony in your ear as the voice stretches across it.
cues.evidence: Visually inspected Durand full score, title and printed pp. 2–7: https://ks15.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/b/bf/IMSLP230262-SIBLEY1802.21472.93de-39087015816665score.pdf. Whole-work listening point, not an assertion that a particular note or entrance occurs at this timestamp.

cues.title: Motion beneath a held line
cues.text: The opening organ part keeps changing beneath the longer vocal notes. Listen for the difference between a sustained melody and an accompaniment that will not quite settle: quietness need not mean harmonic rest.
cues.evidence: Visually inspected Durand full score, printed pp. 2–3: https://ks15.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/b/bf/IMSLP230262-SIBLEY1802.21472.93de-39087015816665score.pdf. Whole-work listening point, not an assertion that a particular note or entrance occurs at this timestamp.

cues.title: Written through her sister
cues.text: Boulanger dictated this last work to Nadia when she could no longer write it herself. The circumstance explains how the score was preserved; it does not tell us what every dissonance was meant to represent.
cues.evidence: Everest insert, Pie Jesu paragraph; also the scholarly biography at https://repertoire-explorer.musikmph.de/wp-content/uploads/vorworte_prefaces/987.html https://i.discogs.com/ecobVEtkndUWiEUEMLY8MtA8w9JdTo5FZXqN58TzXGA/rs:fit/g:sm/q:90/h:598/w:600/czM6Ly9kaXNjb2dz/LWRhdGFiYXNlLWlt/YWdlcy9SLTYwNTY4/NTItMTQ3MzM1MTAw/MC02NTk5LmpwZWc.jpeg

cues.title: Pressure without a chorus
cues.text: The small ensemble reaches a sustained rise in intensity here. Follow the length of the build, then the retreat: the scale of the phrase matters more than the number of performers.
cues.evidence: Actual cached mono stream: cache/analysis/lili-boulanger-pie-jesu.txt, the level rises through roughly 1:35–2:00 before the marked withdrawal near 2:14 Source file: https://archive.org/details/lp_du-fond-de-labime-psaume-24-psaume-129_lili-boulanger-igor-markevitch-orchestre-d. These measurements establish the broad contour, not isolated instruments or words.

cues.title: Room after the crest
cues.text: The sound has drawn back sharply. Listen across the softer passage rather than treating it as a fresh beginning: the return of pressure will grow out of this quieter space.
cues.evidence: Actual cached mono stream: cache/analysis/lili-boulanger-pie-jesu.txt, a strong boundary at 2:14 separates the preceding crest from the quieter 2:15–2:35 windows Source file: https://archive.org/details/lp_du-fond-de-labime-psaume-24-psaume-129_lili-boulanger-igor-markevitch-orchestre-d. These measurements establish the broad contour, not isolated instruments or words.

cues.title: A boy’s solo voice
cues.text: The soloist is Alain Fauqueur of the Petits Chanteurs de Vincennes, not an unnamed soprano and not the album’s adult contralto. The sleeve credits Igor Markevitch as conductor and Nadia Boulanger with recording supervision.
cues.evidence: Roster on the insert front; the individual Pie Jesu heading names Fauqueur on https://i.discogs.com/ecobVEtkndUWiEUEMLY8MtA8w9JdTo5FZXqN58TzXGA/rs:fit/g:sm/q:90/h:598/w:600/czM6Ly9kaXNjb2dz/LWRhdGFiYXNlLWlt/YWdlcy9SLTYwNTY4/NTItMTQ3MzM1MTAw/MC02NTk5LmpwZWc.jpeg https://i.discogs.com/XrNcaeuOsiqmWirxmPgDAtlexW1ImUbc9UpE5Aw4kkg/rs:fit/g:sm/q:90/h:600/w:592/czM6Ly9kaXNjb2dz/LWRhdGFiYXNlLWlt/YWdlcy9SLTYwNTY4/NTItMTQ3MzM1MDk5/Ny02MDQ1LmpwZWc.jpeg

cues.title: A different kind of rest
cues.text: In the closing passage the score turns to G major, slows, and brings in the previously silent harp beside muted strings. Listen for a change of harmonic footing and accompaniment, rather than assuming that repose must mean a lower recorded volume.
cues.evidence: Visually inspected Durand full score, printed pp. 6–7, figure 4, Lent: https://ks15.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/b/bf/IMSLP230262-SIBLEY1802.21472.93de-39087015816665score.pdf. cache/analysis/lili-boulanger-pie-jesu.txt: the level rises from −16.7 dB at 3:15 to −6.9 dB at 3:20, with a structural boundary near 3:24. This contrast anchors the closing region approximately; the G-major identification and quiet written dynamics come from the score, not a claim that this recording suddenly gets softer.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A posthumous score
cues.text: Boulanger died in March 1918, aged twenty-four. Durand published the Pie Jesu after her death; the consulted score carries the original 1922 copyright, although this scan is of a later impression.
cues.evidence: Publication information and score title page; biographical dates: https://guides.loc.gov/feminism-french-women-history/famous/lili-boulanger https://imslp.org/wiki/Pie_Jesu_(Boulanger,_Lili)

cues.title: Leave space for the ending
cues.text: The final sound thins into resonance. Keep listening after the phrase seems complete: the remaining instrumental sound belongs to the ending, not to a new section.
cues.evidence: Actual cached mono stream: cache/analysis/lili-boulanger-pie-jesu.txt, the final windows decline towards the file’s end at 4:46.2; this does not locate the exact vocal release Source file: https://archive.org/details/lp_du-fond-de-labime-psaume-24-psaume-129_lili-boulanger-igor-markevitch-orchestre-d. These measurements establish the broad contour, not isolated instruments or words.

transitions.title: The organ’s unease becomes instrumental
transitions.how: At figure 2 the voice rests while organ and strings carry the tension. The organ’s chromatic motion continues rather than yielding to a clean break, and the strings enlarge the rising line. A crescendo makes the instrumental paragraph an intensification of the prayer, not an unrelated interlude.
transitions.evidence: Visually inspected Durand full score, printed p. 4, figure 2: https://ks15.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/b/bf/IMSLP230262-SIBLEY1802.21472.93de-39087015816665score.pdf. Actual cached analysis, cache/analysis/lili-boulanger-pie-jesu.txt: the rise around 1:34–2:00 supplies the broad anchor. The written mechanism is documented; its placement in this recording is approximate, not a timed word or bar alignment.

transitions.title: A quieter voice answers the crest
transitions.how: The instrumental crest subsides; the returning voice is marked very quiet and plaintive while the organ continues underneath. Strings give way around the renewed vocal phrase. Boulanger changes the balance of the small ensemble rather than stopping the harmonic motion; the later “Un peu animé” lets urgency return within the same prayer.
transitions.evidence: Visually inspected Durand full score, printed pp. 4–5, vocal return and figure 3: https://ks15.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/b/bf/IMSLP230262-SIBLEY1802.21472.93de-39087015816665score.pdf. Actual cached analysis, cache/analysis/lili-boulanger-pie-jesu.txt: the strong 2:14 change and lower subsequent level locate the withdrawal. The written mechanism is documented; its placement in this recording is approximate, not a timed word or bar alignment.

transitions.title: Harp colour accompanies a harmonic release
transitions.how: A pronounced slowing leads into the Lent passage at figure 4. G major replaces the earlier minor-key unease; the harp enters beside muted strings, and the organ supports a more settled bass. The high voice remains central, but its surroundings have changed from restless chromatic motion to a quieter sustained close.
transitions.evidence: Visually inspected Durand full score, printed pp. 6–7, figure 4 and final G-major chord: https://ks15.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/b/bf/IMSLP230262-SIBLEY1802.21472.93de-39087015816665score.pdf. Actual cached analysis, cache/analysis/lili-boulanger-pie-jesu.txt: the level rises sharply out of the 3:15 dip, with a boundary near 3:24; the final withdrawal occurs later, after about 4:10. The score supplies G major, harp entry and slowing. Their placement is approximate, not a timed word or bar alignment.

Representative opening vocal phrase over organ and sustained strings, printed p. 2; entrance time approximate.

composer.epithet: Her songs and psalms give a sustained bass, a repeated interval and the weight of a choral unison the force of a large formal argument.
facts: Daughter of Ernest and Raïssa Boulanger; younger sister of the composer, conductor and teacher Nadia Boulanger
Paris Conservatoire; composition with Paul Vidal, with extensive musical support from Nadia
First woman to win the Premier Grand Prix de Rome for musical composition, 1913
Songs, choral works, orchestral and chamber pieces; unfinished opera La Princesse Maleine
composer.background:
Lili Boulanger grew up in a Paris household where composition, singing and teaching were family work. Her father Ernest had won the Prix de Rome in 1835 and taught singing at the Conservatoire; her mother Raïssa had been his pupil. Nadia, born in 1887, was already receiving serious musical training when Lili was small. Lili learned piano and several other instruments and accompanied her sister into Conservatoire classes. Recurrent illness interrupted her education from childhood. The resulting timetable was irregular, but the musical environment was exceptionally well supplied with teachers, performers and scores.

Nadia was an early mentor and practical support; Lili’s formal composition teacher at the Conservatoire was Paul Vidal. Their training included fugue, harmony and the cantata, extending well beyond the short piano pieces through which women composers were often permitted a public identity. In 1912 illness forced Lili to withdraw from the final stage of the Prix de Rome. She returned in 1913 and won the Premier Grand Prix with Faust et Hélène, becoming the first woman to receive that composition prize. She was nineteen. Nadia had won a second prize in 1908.
